title: Why timing is so hard, and when the entry date matters
objectives: Explain the twice-right problem and why rebounds come when fear is highest.
Say how much the entry date matters at under 1 year, 3–5 years and 7+ years.
body_md:
To time the market, an investor must be right twice: when to get out, and when to get back in. The sharpest rebounds often come soon after the worst falls, when fear is highest, so investors who sell in panic frequently miss them. “Wrong time” depends on the horizon: under 1 year — yes, a lot, which is why equity doesn't belong here. 3–5 years — somewhat; a fall near the end can hurt. 7+ years — much less; time and continued investing smooth out the entry point.

| Horizon | Does the entry date matter much? |
| --- | --- |
| Under 1 year | Yes, a lot. Which is why equity doesn't belong here |
| 3–5 years | Somewhat; a fall near the end can hurt |
| 7+ years | Much less; time and continued investing smooth out the entry point |

> **Talk-track:** “Markets fall regularly; that's normal. The question isn't whether you picked the perfect day. It's whether this money has enough time and the right mix for your goal.”

> **Investor takeaway:** For long-term money, the bigger risk is not investing at the “wrong” time; it's leaving at the wrong time.
example: A client who sold in March 2020 and waited “until it's clear” missed the fastest part of the rebound — timing needs two right calls, not one.
